The Asian koel (Eudynamys scolopaceus) begins life as an altricial nestling hatching from an egg deposited in the nest of a host species. The incubation period for this brood parasite is surprisingly brief; field observations of eggs placed with the long-tailed shrike (Lanius schach), a frequent host, indicate that the young emerge after approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days] when eggs are incubated at a stable temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Upon hatching, the hatchling possesses a modest mass, with neonatal wet weight recorded at just 9.1 grams [Ww0 = 9.1 grams]. This low initial mass is typical of altricial species that rely heavily on parental provisioning for rapid growth and development during the nestling phase. The relatively short incubation period places selective pressure on the koel chick to develop quickly and outcompete host nestlings for food resources delivered by the unwitting foster parents.

Growth proceeds rapidly after emergence from the egg. At the elevated body temperature characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds: fledging occurs at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching], while puberty occurs at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching], and first reproduction is considerably delayed, occurring at 2.1 years after birth [tR = 2.1 years after birth]. This remarkably accelerated development to the fledgling stage allows the young koel to leave the host nest before many host chicks have even begun to fledge, and the rapid maturation to a reproductively capable juvenile is an adaptation that facilitates early breeding in the species.

Adult body size in the Asian koel shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, a feature common among many members of the Cuculidae family. Females ultimately attain a significantly larger body mass than males, with a recorded asymptotic wet weight of 194.92 grams [Wwi = 194.92 grams]. This substantial adult mass contrasts sharply with the modest neonatal weight of 9.1 grams [Ww0 = 9.1 grams], representing a roughly twenty-fold increase during the growth period. The maximum adult mass recorded for females in some populations can reach up to 222 grams [Wwi = 222 grams], though this extreme value may reflect individuals in exceptionally good condition or those carrying fully developed eggs. This size disparity is linked to the energetic demands of egg production and the competitive advantages larger females may have in securing access to high-quality host nests for parasitism. The energy required to develop such a pronounced size difference from a small starting point is substantial, and the rapid growth trajectory is supported by the efficient provisioning behavior of the host parents.

The basal metabolic rate of the Asian koel has been assessed under controlled laboratory conditions. Oxygen consumption measurements taken at a body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] reveal a maximum resting metabolic rate of 296 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 296 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate is consistent with expectations for a bird of this body mass and reflects the energetic costs of maintaining endothermy and supporting the high activity levels required for foraging, territory defense, and the surveillance of potential host nests. The correlation between body size and metabolic rate is well documented, and the koel's BMR aligns with the typical allometric scaling relationships observed among cuckoo species. The elevated metabolic demands are met by a diet rich in fruits and insects, providing the necessary caloric intake to sustain such physiological activity. Lifespan data for this species indicate considerable longevity; the maximum recorded lifespan is 16.6 years [am = 16.6 years] when individuals are maintained under optimal conditions at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C].

Reproductive output in the Asian koel is characterized by a high potential fecundity, which is necessary to compensate for the losses associated with brood parasitism. Females produce approximately 13 eggs per season [Ri = approximately 13 eggs per season], distributing these among multiple host nests to maximize the chances of successful fledging. They typically achieve a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], reflecting the strong seasonal constraints on breeding in many parts of their range. This annual output is a key driver of the species' life-history strategy and is maintained under the same thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] that govern other physiological processes. The long lifespan of 16.6 years [am = 16.6 years] allows individuals to accrue multiple breeding seasons, thereby compensating for the low per-season survival of individual eggs at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This combination of high annual fecundity and extended reproductive tenure is characteristic of many brood-parasitic cuckoos. The maximum daily reproduction rate, implied by the combination of 13 eggs per season and a single clutch per year, equates to approximately 0.036 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 0.036 eggs per day], though this daily rate is less ecologically meaningful than the seasonal and annual metrics.
